text: People used to shave the edges off their coins, and then spend them anyway!
Back then, a silver coin was worth the silver inside it.
So shave a little off a hundred coins, melt the shavings, and you have free silver!
This was called clipping, and you could be put to death for it.
So in sixteen sixty-two, England started making coins by machine, with a pattern pressed into the edge.
Now, if someone shaved a coin, the missing edge gave them away!
But the old, smooth coins were still everywhere.
So in sixteen ninety-six, England melted down its old money and made it all again.
And the man whose job was to catch the cheaters was Isaac Newton!
His biggest target was William Chaloner, a forger who had even learned to fake the edges.
Newton questioned the witnesses himself, and Chaloner was hanged.
Today's coins are not silver. So why keep the ridges?
Partly tradition. But the ridges also help blind people tell coins apart by touch!
So those ridges are a leftover from when people shaved their money!
